conviction_note: The market marked DOO down 10.8% over three sessions (TSX close 93.82 on 21 Aug to 83.67 on 26 Aug) on the US Section 338 50% Canada tariff and Trump's 24 Aug threat, and it is still 8.4% below the 21 Aug close with no BRP-specific clarification in print anywhere; Section 338 explicitly excludes goods already under Section 232, which is exactly what BRP's snowmobiles and most ORV models became on 6 April 2026, and ~75% of BRP units are built in Mexico rather than Canada, so tomorrow's call is the first venue where that carve-out gets said out loud. I size it well below the 6.5% indicative implied move because BRP's observable quarterly prints gap hard then fade (21 May 2026 opened +8.6% premarket and the close-to-close move was under 1%), and because BRP has suspended guidance on a tariff shock once already this year and Trump's threatened 1 Jan 2027 50% on all Canadian vehicles lands one month inside FY27 Q4.

findings.finding: The 50% Section 338 tariff on Canadian imports that took DOO from C$93.82 to C$83.67 between 21 and 26 August explicitly does not apply to goods already subject to Section 232 duties - and BRP's snowmobiles and 'the majority of ORV models' have been Section 232 derivative articles at 25% of full value since 6 April 2026, by BRP's own disclosure.
findings.source_date: 2026-08-22 (effective date stated in document; Section 338 took effect 12:01am ET 22 Aug 2026)
findings.why_not_priced: If the market had worked through the non-stacking carve-out, DOO would not have tracked Magna one-for-one on 24 August (DOO -5.94%, Magna -6.56%) when Magna IS the Section 232 auto/parts complex and BRP is Mexico-origin recreational vehicles already inside Section 232. And the gap would have closed over the following six sessions as trade counsel published the annex analyses - instead DOO closed 2 Sep at 85.90, still 8.4% below the 21 Aug close. A targeted search for any note, wire item or trade-press piece connecting BRP to the Section 232 exclusion returned nothing: BRP has issued no release since 18 August and its next scheduled communication is tomorrow's 09:00 EDT call. Coverage that had priced this would read 'BRP largely exempt from Section 338'; no such sentence exists.
findings.independence: Holland & Knight, a separate firm, states the same exclusion independently and adds that the proclamation named for 'motor vehicles' does not in fact reach vehicles because they are already under Section 232 (https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/07/50-percent-opening-bid-canadian-imports-subject-to-section-338-tariffs). Separately, the Globe and Mail documents that ~75% of BRP units are produced across four Mexican facilities in Juarez and Queretaro with 60% of output sold in the US, so the Canada-origin share of US-bound volume is a minority regardless of the carve-out (https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-us-tariffs-turn-ski-doo-maker-brps-mexico-production-hub-into-a/, 2025-02-03).

findings.finding: BRP has never once mentioned an IEEPA tariff refund - not in the Q1 FY27 call, not in the FY26 financial statements - while Polaris booked US$74m of IEEPA refunds in the exactly-overlapping quarter with ~US$40m more pending, and BRP's own FY26 tariff drag was described as falling 'mainly on PA&A', the Asia-sourced, IEEPA-dutiable and therefore refundable part of its cost base.
findings.why_not_priced: Consensus of $(0.46) sits exactly on BRP's own 28 May guidance of 'earnings to decline by approximately CAD 1.60 to CAD 1.65 year-over-year' - an estimate anchored purely to the Section 232 cost and set before CBP's refund channel, which opened 20 April 2026, had processed anything. Q2 FY27 (1 May - 31 Jul) is BRP's first full quarter inside that window. If the street had modelled a recovery, at least one estimate in a four-estimate sample would sit above the company's own guide rather than on it, and BRP's coverage would frame the name as an IEEPA refund beneficiary rather than exclusively as a Section 232 victim. Every BRP note is about the CAD 500-550m Section 232 number; none is about the refundable pre-February tariff base.
findings.independence: Different company, different document, same refund channel: the Polaris transcript is the evidence that the mechanism is live and being recognised in this exact calendar quarter, and it is independent of BRP's own disclosure. BRP's side of it is the absence in its own Q1 FY27 transcript (https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-brp-inc-q1-2027-surpasses-forecasts-stock-rises-93CH-4714754, 2026-05-28), which mentions no refund, no IEEPA, no Supreme Court and no drawback. Note this finding shares a theme (tariffs) with finding 1 but no source and no legal instrument - Section 338 and IEEPA refunds are separate.

findings.finding: BRP's model-year 2027 ORV price sheet, revealed with the 17 August product launch, holds price increases near 1% and outright lowers prices on selected Can-Am Commander, Defender and Outlander models while adding factory-installed content - i.e. BRP is absorbing the 25% ad valorem tariff in margin rather than pricing it, and its CAD 200m mitigation plan is overhead and lean initiatives, not price.
findings.source_date: 2026-08 (published after BRP's 17 Aug 2026 MY27 reveal; article headline and body describe the MY27 price sheet)
findings.why_not_priced: The actual MY27 price sheet exists only in powersports trade press; it is on no terminal and in no wire preview, which carry the guidance range and the consensus loss instead. If it were priced, H2 gross-margin estimates would already be pinned to the bottom of the CAD 925-975m EBITDA guide and TD would not have moved the name to Buy on 18 August. Cuts against my two positive findings, which is why I keep it.
findings.independence: Partly confirmatory rather than new: the Globe and Mail's 28 May report on the guidance restoration already recorded that BRP planned 'no major U.S. pricing changes' and that the CAD 200m mitigation was overhead and travel (https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-brp-restores-financial-outlook-expects-major-profit-hit-amid-us-tariff/, 2026-05-28). The August price sheet is the confirmation, not the announcement, so I have sized it small and flag that it should not be counted as a second independent margin datapoint.

searched_and_found_nothing: Whether ORVs or snowmobiles got into the 1 June 2026 Section 232 Annex I-C relief (mobile industrial equipment, origin-based 15%/25% and a USMCA value-content formula, effective 8 June). Global Trade Alert lists only forklifts, earth-moving machinery, non-agricultural tractors and mobile cranes; I could not extract the CBP code list, and Powersports Business's tariffs tag has no entry between 23 April and 1 July, which is strong evidence ORVs got nothing - https://globaltradealert.org/blog/s232-metals-update-june-2026 and https://powersportsbusiness.com/tag/tariffs/

Direct confirmation that HTS 8703/8711/8903 are absent from the Section 338 Annex II lists. CBP's own HTS list PDF (https://content.govdelivery.com/attachments/USDHSCBP/2026/08/21/file_attachments/3754630/Section%20338%20Canada%20HTS%20LIST%20Final.pdf) would not render in this environment; I relied on the general Section 232 exclusion instead

Canada's 8 September counter-tariff list including powersports - the Finance Canada release of 25 August names steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics and does not reach 8703/8711/8903, and Moto Canada was still lobbying against inclusion on 25 August, so the competitive windfall against US-assembled OEMs in Canada is not in place - https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/news/2026/08/canada-announces-targeted-countermeasures-and-substantive-support-for-workers-and-businesses-in-response-to-us-tariffs.html

A material new recall or warranty event in the quarter - the May 2026 Can-Am Outlander Pro speed-limiter recall is a sub-one-hour ECM software update, and the Sea-Doo Switch front-overload recall is Bulletin 2026-1 dated 17 October 2025, i.e. already in FY26
Quebec or Mexico layoff/production-cut notices at BRP over the summer - the only Quebec collective dismissal filings I could find are from November 2024
Any 2026 secondary offering, Beaudier/Bain/CDPQ selldown, or NCIB suspension; the December 2025 NCIB renewal runs to 9 December 2026 and I found no change
A credit rating action in June-August 2026; net leverage was 1.8x at Q4 FY26 and the October 2025 term loan repricing is the last balance-sheet event I could source
FX as a distinct edge - USD/CAD sat around 1.376-1.39 through the quarter versus roughly 1.37-1.38 a year earlier, a mild translation tailwind but nowhere near a finding, and BRP hedges forward
Any signal that July retail deteriorated - Polaris said July tracked consistent with Q2, utility strong and recreational soft, which is a read-through already public since 28 July
baseline_tension: Cuts against the run-up: the 20-day tape reads flat at -1.23% only because a +7.74% TD-upgrade day on 18 August was fully given back in the 24-26 August Canada-tariff selloff, and my primary finding says that specific selloff over-marked BRP for a duty its products are carved out of - meanwhile the option chain offers no contradiction, with skew null, put/call open interest at 0.01 on 7,102 contracts and an ATM spread 65% of mid, so there is no market statement of direction here to disagree with.
